summary: This paper develops a general theoretical framework for understanding qubit measurement and backaction in multimode nonreciprocal readout networks, and experimentally implements a three-mode parametric device to validate the theory. The work extends phase-space methods to handle arbitrary networks of linearly coupled modes with embedded qubits, demonstrating quantitative agreement between measured and predicted measurement rates and dephasing with no free parameters.
motivation: Ferrite circulators limit scalability of superconducting quantum processors due to their size, loss, and magnetic field requirements. Networks of parametrically coupled modes offer a promising integrated alternative, but the coupled qubit-readout system lacks quantitative theoretical understanding needed for optimization.
method: The authors develop a Wigner function formalism for computing qubit dephasing as parasitic and measurement-induced contributions from multimode Gaussian states, decomposing dephasing into terms depending on mode variance and displacement. They implement this theory in a hybrid device with a transmon qubit, a $\lambda/4$ coaxial cavity (mode C), and a chip with amplifier (mode A) and buffer (mode B) modes coupled via a dc SQUID, characterizing all parameters via catch-and-release protocols and performing simultaneous $T_1$ and $T_2$ echo measurements.
result: For the three-mode interferometer at $\phi = \pm\pi/2$, measurement efficiency reached $\eta \approx 7\%$ (limited by downstream added noise of $\bar{n}_{\mathrm{rest}} \approx 5.24$ quanta), with excellent agreement between measured and theoretical $\Gamma_{\mathrm{meas}}$ and $\Gamma_d$. Theory predicts that with gain ($\mathcal{G}_{BB} = 20$ dB) the same device parameters yield $\eta < 97.5\%$ in the infinite-gain limit, constrained by cooperativities and stability criteria from Eq. (37): $\mathcal{C}_\lambda < 1 + \mathcal{C}_{AB}$.
